data_section_full_text:
4.2 FINANCIAL DATA AND SAMPLE SELECTION

Table 1 describes the sample-selection processes. From a total of 77,953
firm-year observations available on Worldscope for the sample countries,
pre-1990 financial data are deleted because ownership and control structures earlier than 1991 may differ from those documented for 1996 to 1999.
Observations for financial institutions are also removed because the financial variables used in their income management measures are not comparable to those used by industrial firms (14,745 observations). Firm-years with
negative values for non-negative items (sales, depreciation, accumulated depreciation, and cash and marketable securities) are deleted to ensure the
accuracy of the income management proxy (15,494 observations). <sup>14</sup> The
cross-sectional Jones [1991] model application further removes observations that do not cover three consecutive years with the same fiscal year-end
for the estimation of cash flows from operations (517 observations); observations that have missing values for either change in revenues or gross
property, plant, and equipment, both deflated by lagged total assets (6,957
observations); observations that fall in the top or bottom 1% of extreme
observations of the model variables (2,866 observations); and observations
that belong to two-digit SIC industries with fewer than eight firms in a particular year (417 observations). The final sample consists of 25,210 observations, after merging the financial data with the ownership sample, which is
equivalent to 73.6% of the observations in the previous step. <sup>15</sup> This suggests

13 The use of the number of domestic firms divided by population (La Porta et al. [1998])
as an alternative proxy yields similar results.

14 A comparison of randomly selected firms from the final sample with the data from Global
Vantage (an international version of Standard & Poor’s Compustat) shows that the financial
data are accurate, mitigating any concern about the accuracy of the remaining sample.

15 Samplefirmsarelarger,moreprofitable(intermsofreturnonassets),lessrisky(in financial
leverage and systematic risk), and are more likely to be in regulated industries than excluded
firms. Furthermore, sample firms exhibit significantly smaller abnormal accruals with a mean
(median) DACC of −0.003 (−0.002) than excluded firms, with a mean (median) DACC of
0.005 (0.004). However, the magnitude of the abnormal accruals is significantly larger for
sample firms (mean | DACC | = 0.051) than for excluded firms (mean | DACC | = 0.047). To the
extent that smaller firms drop out more frequently (because of greater data-collection costs
for smaller firms), | DACC | ( Diverge ) is likely to be understated (overstated) because firm size is
negatively correlated with | DACC | and is positively correlated with Diverge . These biases would
